The report you are pointing to does not show “staggering fraud” in the ACA. It describes data-matching and enrollment integrity issues that federal agencies already monitor and routinely correct. These are not findings of proven fraud on a massive scale, and they are not evidence that insurers were knowingly paid for nonexistent people. In many cases, payments are provisional and later reconciled, with insurers required to return money when eligibility is not confirmed. That process is built into the ACA by design.

The “$94 million sent to insurers for the deceased” claim is especially misleading. That figure reflects preliminary payments tied to records that had not yet been updated across multiple federal databases. When deaths are confirmed, payments are clawed back. This is not unique to the ACA and happens across Medicare, Medicaid, Social Security, and private employer insurance. Using this number as evidence of rampant fraud ignores the fact that reconciliation and recovery are already required by law.

The claim about 68,000 Social Security numbers being used by multiple people also does not mean 68,000 cases of fraud. Duplicate or mismatched SSNs often result from data entry errors, name changes, family coverage overlaps, immigration documentation timing, or identity verification delays. Auditors explicitly note that duplicates are not proof of fraudulent enrollment unless intent and false claims are established, which this report does not do.

Most importantly, the narrative about “pouring billions into insurance companies” is false. ACA subsidies go to the insured, not to insurers. Insurers are legally required to spend at least 80 percent to 85 percent of premium dollars on actual medical care. If they do not, they must issue rebates to consumers. That rule disappears if Republicans succeed in dismantling the ACA, which would actually increase insurer profits while raising premiums.

Republicans also do not have a serious plan to lower costs. Letting ACA subsidies expire raises premiums by double or triple for millions of people starting in January and would drive many out of coverage entirely. That does not lower costs, it shifts them onto families, hospitals, and state budgets while increasing uncompensated care.

This is not a fraud scandal. It is a familiar political tactic, exaggerate routine administrative issues, strip away consumer protections, and then blame the system for the damage that follows.
